papers.title: Shuffle squares in smooth binary words and the Kolakoski sequence
papers.abstract: A binary word is a shuffle square if its positions can be partitioned into two identical subsequences. A finite word over $\{1,2\}$ is smooth if repeated finite run-length differentiation remains binary until the empty word is reached. This paper proves that every smooth binary word in which both letters have even multiplicity is a shuffle square once its length is at least $18$. There are exactly $34$ exceptions, all of length at most $16$. The infinite part of the proof is a parity-return atom induction: a smooth even-Parikh word factors uniquely into smooth parity atoms, and every such atom has length at most $8$. A finite, independently checkable certificate handles lengths $18$ through $40$. As a consequence, a nonempty prefix of the classical Kolakoski sequence is a shuffle square if and only if both symbols occur an even number of times and its length is not $4$ or $8$. There are infinitely many such prefixes. In fact, the entire infinite Kolakoski sequence can be partitioned into two identical infinite subsequences with monochromatic blocks of uniformly bounded length.

papers.title: Small universal multiset reaction systems
papers.abstract: This paper presents a construction of a small universal machine within the framework of Multi-set Reaction Systems. We encode the machine state using elements that represent registers and instruction labels, and we enforce sequential execution by ensuring that reaction chains for a given instruction can only activate after the corresponding label element appears. We implement a universal register machine with 8 registers and 23 instructions, showing that the priority-based model requires 87 distinct elements. The results demonstrate that multiset reaction systems are capable of simulating universal computation.

papers.title: $\Psi$-TM: An Exact Rounds-versus-Queries Trade-off for Pointer Chasing, Machine-Checked in Lean 4
papers.abstract: An algorithm that reads its input through queries is adaptive if it may choose a query after seeing the answers to earlier ones. We ask how much adaptivity is worth when queries are issued in rounds. In the model, called $\Psi$-TM, the input is reachable only through an interface that returns the content of a queried cell; in each round an algorithm submits a batch of cells, chosen from the answers of earlier rounds only. Depth is the number of rounds and cost is the number of cells read, as for deterministic decision trees of bounded adaptivity. For $k$-step pointer chasing over $k$ tables of $m \geq 2$ entries we determine the cost at every depth: for $1 \leq d \leq k$, the least worst-case number of reads of a deterministic algorithm with at most $d$ rounds is exactly $(k-d)m+d$. Each round removed costs exactly $m-1$ additional reads; $k$ rounds need $k$ reads, $k-1$ rounds need $m+k-1$ (for $k \geq 2$), and no algorithm without rounds decides the problem. The lower bound comes from an adversary that answers every query to entry $a$ of a table with $a$ itself, except at the first unread cell of the chain, which it uses to steer the chain to a cell the algorithm has not read. The query model, the problem and the theorem, for every number of rounds, are formalised in Lean 4 without Mathlib; the proofs contain no sorry and use only the axioms propext and Quot.sound. An exhaustive search over all strategies confirms the formula independently for small parameters.
